name: Warrnambool language
confidence_why: Blake 2003 reports only that Tyers's 1842 wordlist (printed 1878) and Lindsay's notation put the accent on the final syllable of two-syllable words and scatter it across longer ones, while Hercus 1986 transcribes the last Lake Condah speaker with initial stress on every word, so no placement can be stated with any confidence.

catalog_quote: [Blake 2003:28-29] In the majority of Australian languages word stress (or accent) falls on the first syllable, but there are exceptions, one of them being Mathi-Mathi, where the stress in words of more than two syllables falls on various syllables according to certain principles (Hercus 1986d:115). Tyers marks stress and it appears that stress falls regularly on the final syllable of disyllabic words, of which there are numerous examples. [p. 29] karrìp thigh / bebì father / werìte banksia / kannòc waddy / There are a few examples of longer words with stress marked variously. Lindsay also marks stress. In his notation, stress on disyllabic words is predominantly on the second syllable. As with Tyers, stress on longer words appears on various syllables. ... [Hercus 1986:159-160] Only tentative remarks can be made on the phonetics and allophonic variations observed: ... Very noticeable was the long and tense articulation of intervocalic m, particularly when it followed the accented vowel: ... ḏamon meat, dameri sheep and ŋamadjidj white man were therefore transcribed phonetically as [ˈθammɔn], [ˈtammerI] and [ˈŋammatjItj]. ... After an unaccented vowel m did not appear to be geminated: guremug [ˈkurəmUk] possum. ... before ŋ, a was pronounced as an unrounded back vowel [ɑ] as in [ˈmalɑŋ] girl [ˈdelɑŋ] stringy-bark.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Section 2.3.6 'Stress' begins at the foot of book p. 28 (p. 42) and runs onto p. 29 (p. 43). The quoted passage is there word for word: 'In the majority of Australian languages word stress (or accent) falls on the first syllable, but there are exceptions, one of them being Mathi-Mathi, where the stress in words of more than two syllables falls on various syllables according to certain principles (Hercus 1986d:115). new_statements.rule_in_words: Blake's consolidated grammar (the only modern description) has no speaker data; it reports that two 19th-century recorders (Tyers 1878, Lindsay 1892) marked stress on the final/second syllable of disyllables and inconsistently on longer words, and he notes this departs from the usual Australian initial-stress pattern. Hercus 1986:159-160, the one source with phonetic notes from an actual (last) speaker, transcribes every 2-3-syllable word with initial stress ([ˈθammɔn], [ˈkurəmUk], [ˈŋammatjItj], [ˈmalaŋ]..) and refers to gemination after 'the accented vowel' (first syllable). Taken together: final stress in disyllables per 19th-century orthographies vs initial stress per 1962-3 phonetic notes — no settled rule; if the catalog must pick one, Blake's own reading is 'final in disyllables, variable in longer words' (closest fixed-list label fixed: final syllable, but Blake hedges with 'it appears').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Blake; Hercus gives no secondary marks for Gundidj (her 'secondary stress' remarks in the same volume concern other languages).
new_statements.exceptions: Blake: words of more than two syllables have stress 'marked variously' / 'on various syllables' in both Tyers and Lindsay; Lindsay's disyllables only 'predominantly' second-syllable. Hercus's initial-stress transcriptions from Mr Alberts conflict with the 19th-century marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from 19th-century vocabularies (Tyers' Glenelg/Wannon area list, Lindsay's Lake Condah notes); Hercus's fragments are isolated words from Lake Condah dialect. Note Blake §1.4.3: almost all nouns are consonant-final (historical loss of final vowels), which may bear on the second-syllable marks in disyllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Blake 2003 covers the whole Warrnambool language (dialects Kuurn Kopan Noot, Peek Whurrong, Wuluwurrung, Pikwurrung, etc; Mathews' 'Dhauhurtwurru'); the stress marks come from Tyers (Glenelg/Wannon area, western dialects) and Lindsay (Lake Condah). Hercus 1986 §6.1 'Gundidj' = Lake Condah dialect fragments from Mr Angus Alberts, 1962-3. Language name in Glottolog is 'Warrnambool' (warr1257); community name Gunditjmara / Dhauwurd Wurrung / Keerraywoorroong. The scan's named source (Blake 2003 §2.3.6) was retrieved from the ANU Open Research repository (handle 1885/146713), not sealang.

I read all three page scan: the legend at the foot of p. 66 reads exactly 'Explanation of Symbols used to Point out the Pronunciation. a-circumflex as in "cart." a-grave accented.' and every p. 64 form in the quote (Nerlàng, Kernìng, Wullòng, Kolân, Mring, Karpòng, Tùng-ung, Bollàwing or werràng, Torràide or werrìp, Karrìp, Denòng or tenòng, Nurròke, Murrùng or murràng, Narràng, Mundòl, Mòn-bòng, Kà-loin, Pòpòpe,…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the primary source behind the catalog's existing statement (Blake 2003 §2.3.6, which says 'Tyers marks stress and it appears that stress falls regularly on the final syllable of disyllabic words.. There are a few examples of longer words with stress marked variously'). Reading Tyers directly confirms Blake's summary and adds the actual marked forms and the legend defining the grave accent as 'accented' (vs. circumflex = length as in 'cart'). It does not contradict the catalog's 'unclear or contradictory' reading for the language as a whole, since polysyllables are marked variously, but it sharpens it: for disyllables the 19th-century record is consistently final.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tyers gives no rule in prose; he defines the grave accent as 'accented' and marks it on the vowels of his 1842 wordlist. In the disyllables the mark falls on the last syllable in the great majority of cases (Nerlàng, Kernìng, Wullòng, Karpòng, werràng, Karrìp, Murrùng, Narràng, Werròng, Werrìng, Terlìng, Worròc, Naupùng, Mundòl, Kol-kòn, Nerpùng, Bebì, Korprìng, Wee-làng, Kooròng, Turròot, Perròok, Eròok, Noo-tòng, Kunnòc, Koròne, Koo-wìn, Wat-tài, Wan-denòng, and others on pp. 64-65). Longer words are marked variously: penultimate (Bollàwing, Torràide, Koolòying, kummae-mèrring, Bungàirie, Murro càrra), final (Karra-mòok, Wot-a-wèet, Ma-na-parreèt, Proë-wun-nàl, La-cannòo, Yun-a-kàh, Wen-a-pà, Kree-pin-narràng), initial (Nùrrun-gooroc, Tàiril-kripeer) or two marks. The circumflex is a length mark ('as in cart'), not stress (Kolân, Gorâng, Pârreek, Mâ-trong, Moo-tâng).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No statement. Several words carry two grave accents (Mòn-bòng 'sky', Pòpòpe 'male child', Nùrrajùg 'wind', Kà-kà-tirring 'stars', Wàrren-èet 'wild duck', Kàrra-wàrren 'large wild duck', Yù-a-pàh 'no', Po-lìng-pà-tà 'childbirth', Murrùndie-weèring 'bullock'), which could be read as a second prominence, but Tyers does not say so.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables with a non-final mark: Tùng-ung 'teeth', Kà-loin 'heat or hot', Nurròke 'calf of leg', Karpìne 'rain' (if pi-ne is two syllables). Many words carry no mark at all (Mring, Perrong, Tirring, Karl, Kolul, Lang, Yung, Tring, Woorn, Kinning, Leep, Wurrowing, Gattom-gattom). Longer words are marked on various syllables, as Blake 2003:28-29 already observed.
new_statements.identity_note: Tyers's vocabulary is from 'the tribes inhabiting the country about the Rivers Crawford, Stokes, and lower parts of the Wannon and Glenelg', i.e. the western (Glenelg/Wannon) end of the Warrnambool-language area; Blake 2003 treats it as a source for the same language (his 'Warrnambool language', ISO gjm). Compiled in 1842 by C. J. Tyers, surveyor, printed by Brough Smyth in 1878.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources: Tyers's marks (1842, printed 1878) are exactly what Blake 2003 summarises, and Blake reports that Lindsay's independent notation likewise puts stress predominantly on the second syllable of disyllables. The tension is internal to the data: the disyllables are almost uniformly marked on the final syllable, whereas words of three or more syllables are marked on various syllables (initial, penultimate, final, or twice), and a number of words carry no mark. Blake's general remark that most Australian languages stress the first syllable is stated as background, not as a claim about this language. So 'fixed: final syllable' is well supported only for disyllables; a reviewer who weights the polysyllabic scatter more heavily would keep the catalog's 'unclear or contradictory'.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.6 'Stress', pp. 28-29: based on 19th-century recorders' stress marks — Tyers (1878): stress 'regularly on the final syllable of disyllabic words' (karrìp 'thigh', bebì 'father', werìte 'banksia', kannòc 'waddy'), longer words marked variously; Lindsay (1892): disyllables predominantly second-syllable, longer words on various syllables. Blake contrasts this with the usual Australian initial-stress pattern; no modern speaker data.

sources.note: No explicit stress rule ('only tentative remarks can be made on the phonetics'), but every phonetic transcription from the last rememberer carries an initial stress mark: [ˈθammɔn] 'meat', [ˈtammerI] 'sheep', [ˈŋammatjItj] 'white man', [ˈkurəmUk] 'possum', [ˈbembai] 'bread', [ˈmoe] 'black duck', [ˈmalaŋ] 'girl', [ˈdelaŋ] 'stringy-bark'; text refers to intervocalic m being geminated 'when it followed the accented vowel' and not 'after an unaccented vowel' (guremug). Implies initial accent in the Lake Condah fragments — contradicting the 19th-century final-stress marks Blake reports.

sources.note: Introductory Note: English orthographic rules 'have been necessarily laid aside, together with the signs of accentuation. Double consonants are used to express emphasis, and double vowels to express prolongation of the sound' — i.e. the main 19th-century source deliberately marks no stress; no rule stated.
